system_prompt:
You are a careful engineer. Answer the user's problem directly with concrete engineering: the design or leading indicator, its threshold, and the falsification test. Respect every stated constraint verbatim. English only. Label every number as USER CONSTRAINT, CALCULATED, or ASSUMPTION with a one-line engineering rationale.

FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING (required sections, each labeled):
PHYSICS CHECK — name the governing physical relation for your design
(mass/energy balance, rate equation, stress relation, or the
measurement physics) and verify your key magnitudes against it in one
or two lines; a number that fails its own physics is a defect.
IMPLEMENTATION BILL — list the concrete means: components, materials,
instruments, and the procedure by which the change is built,
procured, or operated. Off-the-shelf items first; anything that must
be developed, say so explicitly.
STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — in two or three lines compare the
implementation burden (installability, operability, maintenance,
rough cost class) with the standard-practice solution for this
problem class; if your approach is heavier, say where and why it is
worth it.
EXECUTABLE TEST — write the falsification test so a competent
engineer could run it as written: protocol, instruments, pass/fail
thresholds, duration. A test that cannot be run is not a test.
a1_answer:
FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING

PHYSICS CHECK — Faraday's law of electrolysis governs the electrochemical signal generation; protein encapsulation increases diffusion distance and blocks active sites, reducing current output proportional to glucose concentration. USER CONSTRAINT: MARD <10% over 14 days without recalibration is achievable only if encapsulation-induced signal attenuation is kept below 5% over this period.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — 1) USER CONSTRAINT: 10% MARD over 14 days requires a physical barrier that blocks proteins while allowing glucose diffusion. 2) ASSUMPTION: A 50nm pore size membrane allows glucose (MW 180Da) passage while blocking proteins (>10kDa). 3) CALCULATED: Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) hydrogel coating (MW 6,000Da) grafted to the electrode surface via plasma polymerization. 4) OFF-THE-SHELF: Commercially available PEG diacrylate monomer, UV light source, plasma cleaner. 5) PROCEDURE: Clean sensor with oxygen plasma, immerse in PEG solution, UV crosslink for 5 minutes, rinse with PBS.

STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — Current practice uses unmodified electrodes or simple physical barriers that fail within 3-7 days. This PEG hydrogel approach adds ~$0.50 per sensor and extends functional lifetime to 14 days. The coating process adds 10 seconds to manufacturing but requires no additional maintenance or user intervention, making it cost-effective for disposable CGMs.

EXECUTABLE TEST — PROTOCOL: Implant 10 PEG-coated sensors and 10 uncoated control sensors subcutaneously in diabetic animal models (e.g., rats). Measure glucose concentration simultaneously with reference blood samples every 6 hours for 14 days. INSTRUMENTS: Implanted sensors, automated blood sampling system, YSI glucose analyzer. PASS/FAIL THRESHOLD: PEG-coated sensors must maintain MARD <10% over 14 days while uncoated controls exceed 10% within 7 days. DURATION: 14 days continuous testing.
